newsitem.title: UK: GOLF - Troon will test Nobilo's mental strength.
newsitem.headline: GOLF - Troon will test Nobilo's mental strength.

text.p: LONDON, July 16 - New Zealand's Frank Nobilo returns to his roots as a professional golfer this week with the task of underlining his new status at the British Open, NZPA reports.

The Aucklander has made a major impact on the United States PGA Tour since moving there full time this season. He has risen into the top 25 of world rankings after winning one and finishing runner-up in another tournament on the American tour.
It is in Europe, though, that Nobilo first came to prominence as a professional.

Despite winning tournaments in Europe and being a regular finisher in the top 20 money earners, Nobilo didn't carve out the same reputation and ascend to the same heights as he has in his first full season in the United States.

Nobilo won the Greater Greensboro Chrysler Classic, then in his most recent outing, a perfect tune-up for the Open, Nobilo finished three strokes behind Tiger Woods in the Motorola Western Open. He has already passed the $1 million earnings barrier this season and looks destined to go higher.
Nobilo appears at ease in the States, where he has already won back-to-back titles in the Sarazen World Championship.
Perhaps that is a reflection of Nobilo's greater maturity as a player, or a product of his increasing confidence and comfort playing alongside the world's top players week in and week out.
Whatever the reason, the expectations are on Nobilo to do well this week, both from his supporters and from himself, in a tournament which he has yet to figure significantly in.
Certainly he has the technical ability. Now he also has the confidence.

The only question over Nobilo is whether he has the mental application to put together four low scores in a high-pressure tournament containing the world's top players. The Sarazen is a big-money tournament, but it is not a major and does not carry the same pressures.
Nobilo has already proven he has what it takes to compete in majors in the United States, finishing fourth in the Masters last year.

But the British Open is a tournament in which Nobilo has not matched the achievements of countrymen Greg Turner, who led after the first round in 1993 and was joint seventh last year, and even Michael Campbell, who was third at St Andrews in 1995 after leading the field going into the final round.
His best has been a share of 11th in 1994.
Nobilo has taken his usual path to a major, taking the previous weekend off which this year meant missing the Loch Lomond Invitational, won by American Tom Lehman.

Lehman is the defending Open champion and one of the favourites this week with the ever-present Woods, U.S. Open champion Ernie Els and Europe's top player Colin Montgomerie, who is playing on his home course.
This year Nobilo even gave up his other sporting passion, motor racing in the form of the British Grand Prix at Silverstone, for the more sedate demands of moving house last weekend.
That may have been physically demanding, but has left him mentally fresh for the Open.
Nobilo is one of three New Zealanders in the field this year, along with Turner and rookie Michael Long.

Turner has been having his trade-mark solid season and this year avoided the rigours of having to qualify for the field, an experience he described as "like going to the dentist without anaesthetic". Last year he did that, and went on to share seventh place in the tournament to earn his 1997 exemption.
Long has no track record in the tournament, but like Nobilo has a new reputation to protect and, he hopes, enhance at Royal Troon.
Long has already secured his European Tour card for 1998 and has risen to No 91 in the official Sony world rankings, but has never played a major.
He hopes to finish in the top 15 to secure an exemption for the 1998 tournament. If he achieves that Long knows he may well find himself in contention for major honours.
Sadly the three exempt New Zealand players are not joined by qualifiers this year, most significantly meaning the absence of Campbell from the field.

That completes a rapid decline from the heights of 1995, when he finished third, through last year, when he was disqualified for failing to correctly mark his card and missed the cut regardless, and now failing to qualify.
The tournament is also without the presence of New Zealand great Bob Charles, the left-hander who won in 1963, who has decided not to exercise his exemption this year.
Charles aims to make his farewell British Open appearance at St Andrews in 2000, and is deciding year-by-year whether to play the intervening tournaments.
This year he has decided against it.
